displayQuote: He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how

meta.title: Who really said "He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nietzsche wrote it — Twilight of the Idols (1889), Maxims and Arrows 12. Frankl quoted him and said so. The famous English is his translator's, 1959.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Frankl's line — he credited Nietzsche both times he used it. The English everyone quotes is Ilse Lasch's 1959 translation of Frankl, not of Nietzsche.

answer.label: Not Viktor Frankl — actually Friedrich Nietzsche
answer.sourceLine: The aphorism is Nietzsche’s: Götzen-Dämmerung (Twilight of the Idols), ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ (Maxims and Arrows) No. 12 — “Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?” Frankl did use the line, twice, in Man’s Search for Meaning, and named Nietzsche both times. The reason it now travels under Frankl’s name is that the English wording is his book’s: it is Ilse Lasch’s 1959 translation of Frankl quoting Nietzsche, not any translation of Nietzsche — and the popular form has since dropped Lasch’s ‘for.’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Götzen-Dämmerung (Twilight of the Idols), ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ No. 12
Drafted 26 August – 3 September 1888; published 1889 (Leipzig: C. G. Naumann), in German
The popular English is Ilse Lasch’s (1959 copyright) — translating Frankl, not Nietzsche. Free English: Ludovici, 1911

source.excerpt: Mit einem Ziele. — Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? — Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das.
trail: The German is the primary text. Project Gutenberg’s Götzen-Dämmerung prints No. 12 as ‘Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? — Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das,’ and Wikiquote lists the same aphorism as Maxims and Arrows § 1.12 German text ↗.

No Nietzsche translator wrote the famous sentence. Ludovici’s 1911 English, edited by Oscar Levy for the Complete Works, gives No. 12 as ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself’ — a rendering with no ‘why,’ no ‘how’ and no ‘bear’ in it at all Ludovici 1911 ↗.

The wording in circulation comes instead from Frankl’s book. Quote Investigator reproduces part one of Man’s Search for Meaning, translated by Ilse Lasch: ‘Nietzsche’s words, “He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how,” could be the guiding motto…’ — and concludes that Nietzsche should receive the credit Quote Investigator ↗.

That translation is Frankl’s publisher’s, not Nietzsche’s. Frankl’s book appeared in German in 1946; the English came out in 1959 as From Death-Camp to Existentialism, with part one translated by Ilse Lasch and Beacon Press as the English publisher publication history ↗.
source.excerptNote: ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ No. 12, entire, in Nietzsche’s German. The famous half is the first clause; the second is a jab at English utilitarianism that quotation almost always discards.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Viktor E. Frankl and the publishers of the Ilse Lasch translation (Beacon Press in the US) — for the English wording only
source.rightsNote: Split, and this is the part people get wrong. Nietzsche’s German is public domain — published 1889, and he died in 1900 — so the original may be quoted and translated freely. But the English sentence you are about to reuse is not from a Nietzsche translation and is still in copyright: it descends from Ilse Lasch’s rendering of Frankl, whose translation copyright is dated 1959. Kaufmann’s and Hollingdale’s Nietzsche translations are also protected. For a free English text use Ludovici’s 1911 translation — ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself’ — or translate the German yourself. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (15 October 1844 – 25 August 1900) began as a classical philologist and turned to philosophy. He drafted Twilight of the Idols in a little over a week — 26 August to 3 September 1888 — and it was printed and bound by January 1889, the month he suffered the breakdown in Turin that ended his working life. Its opening section, ‘Maxims and Arrows,’ is a run of forty-four one-line provocations; this is the twelfth. Its modern fame is largely secondhand, arriving through Man’s Search for Meaning rather than through Nietzsche’s own translators.

misattribution.heading: Right book, wrong author
misattribution.intro: Frankl is credited because the sentence people quote really does come out of his book — but he was quoting, and he said so, in the same breath, twice.

items.why: Both appearances in Man’s Search for Meaning name the source. Part one: ‘Nietzsche’s words, “He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how,” could be the guiding motto…’ Part two: ‘There is much wisdom in the words of Nietzsche…’ Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that Frankl used the saying but credited Nietzsche the investigation ↗.

items.tag: translator of Frankl, not of Nietzsche
items.why: ‘He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how’ is Lasch’s English in part one of Frankl’s book. No Nietzsche translator produced that sentence: Common has ‘wherefore of life,’ Ludovici ‘the manner of it can take care of itself,’ Kaufmann ‘we shall get along with almost any how,’ Hollingdale ‘put up with almost any how’ side-by-side renderings ↗.

The version that spreads has lost Lasch’s ‘for’ while keeping her ‘with’ — a hybrid that is neither Nietzsche nor a clean quotation of Frankl’s page. Frankl’s part two uses a third form: ‘can bear almost any how’ both Frankl passages ↗.

Goodreads runs ‘He who has a Why to live for can bear almost any How’ under the byline ‘— Viktor E. Frankl’ with no mention of Nietzsche anywhere on the page — which is how a quotation loses its author the attribution as displayed ↗.

The aphorism does not end where the quotation ends. It continues: ‘Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das’ — man does not strive after happiness, only the Englishman does that German original ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote it — Götzen-Dämmerung (1889), ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ No. 12. Frankl quoted it and credited him; what Frankl’s book supplied was the English Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it travels under the wrong name
lead: Frankl is the reason most people know the sentence at all. In part one of Man’s Search for Meaning he introduces it while arguing that restoring a prisoner’s inner strength meant first showing him some future goal, and calls Nietzsche’s words a possible ‘guiding motto’ for psychotherapeutic work with prisoners. In part two he returns to it as a motto that ‘holds true for any psychotherapy.’ Both times the credit to Nietzsche is right there in the sentence.

Nietzsche’s own use was lighter and considerably more sardonic. The aphorism sits in a run of one-line jabs and immediately turns into a joke: man does not strive after happiness, only the Englishman does that. Quotation keeps the first clause, drops the punchline, and a barbed aside becomes pure uplift.
context.detailsSummary: Six versions of the same sentence
detailsBody: German (1889): ‘Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? — Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das.’
Thomas Common, 1896 edition: ‘When one has one’s wherefore of life, one gets along with almost every how.’
Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911 edition: ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.’
Walter Kaufmann, in The Portable Nietzsche: ‘If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how.’
R. J. Hollingdale, in the Penguin Twilight of the Idols and The Anti-Christ: ‘If we possess our why of life we can put up with almost any how.’

Ilse Lasch, translating Frankl, part one: ‘He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how’ — and in part two, ‘He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.’ The circulating form is the first of these with ‘for’ knocked out.
context.pull: The Nietzsche line everyone knows is Frankl's translator's English.

sourcesVerified.claim: Nietzsche published the aphorism in German in 1889 in Götzen-Dämmerung, section 'Sprüche und Pfeile'; QI's conclusion is that Nietzsche should receive credit and that Frankl used the saying but credited Nietzsche. QI reproduces Common (1896), Ludovici (1911), Kaufmann (The Portable Nietzsche) and Hollingdale (Penguin) renderings, and both Frankl passages in Ilse Lasch's translation — 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how' (part one) and 'He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how' (part two). QI's bibliography gives the 1889 catalog record as C. G. Naumann, Leipzig, and the Lasch translation as 1959 copyright, 1946 first German publication.

Project Gutenberg's German text of Götzen-Dämmerung prints aphorism 12 of 'Sprüche und Pfeile' verbatim as 'Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? - Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer thut das.'

Project Gutenberg's The Twilight of the Idols, translated by Anthony M. Ludovici, edited by Dr Oscar Levy, volume 16 of the Complete Works (1911), gives 'Maxims and Missiles' no. 12 as 'If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.'

Wikiquote's Friedrich Nietzsche page lists the aphorism under Twilight of the Idols (1889), 'Maxims and Arrows' § 1.12, with the German 'Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?'

Man's Search for Meaning was first published in German in 1946 as Ein Psychologe erlebt das Konzentrationslager; the first English version, From Death-Camp to Existentialism, appeared in the US in 1959, with part one translated by Ilse Lasch and Beacon Press as the English-language publisher.
Goodreads displays 'He who has a Why to live for can bear almost any How' attributed simply to '― Viktor E. Frankl', with no mention of Nietzsche anywhere in the attribution or on the page.
Twilight of the Idols was written between 26 August and 3 September 1888 at Sils Maria and published in 1889; the 'Maxims and Arrows' section comprises 44 concise statements.

Nietzsche lived 15 October 1844 – 25 August 1900, was a German philosopher and writer who began as a classical philologist, suffered a mental breakdown in Turin on 3 January 1889, and Twilight of the Idols was already printed and bound by January 1889 when it was released during his illness.
Internet Archive item 'werkeniet08niet' is Nietzsche's Werke, volume 8 of 11 (Leipzig, 1896), containing Götzen-Dämmerung, freely downloadable in PDF, EPUB and text.
